title: Semaphores, mutexes, and deadlocks

spans.text: LESSON PURPOSE

Goal: apply “Semaphores, mutexes, and deadlocks” to a real program or device. The key principle is: A mutex protects a short critical section; a queue transfers values, so they solve different problems. In a project, follow this guidance: Acquire before shared access and release on every path after a successful take.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
EXAMPLE CODE
EXPECTED RESULT
Serial Monitor prints the shared counter while a mutex protects reads and writes.
CORE EXPLANATION

A semaphore coordinates events or a count of resources; a mutex protects shared mutable state and has ownership and priority-inheritance semantics. Hold a mutex briefly, release it around blocking I/O, and keep lock order consistent to reduce deadlock and priority-inversion risk. Never take a mutex from an ISR.
IMPORTANT LINE BREAKDOWN
Key line:
void writer(void*) { for (;;) { if (xSemaphoreTake(mutex, pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)) == pdTRUE) { ++sharedValue; xSemaphoreGive(mutex); } vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(250)); } }

What it does: A mutex protects a short critical section; a queue transfers values, so they solve different problems.
Why it is used: Acquire before shared access and release on every path after a successful take.
If omitted or changed: Forgetting to release a lock can block tasks indefinitely; check every error and early-return path.
